message: docs: state the flat Diagnostic and the one rule record in every document that still describes the deleted ownership map

edits.find: `contract/diagnostic-ids.ts` owns which of those rules name ids, and the three groups are derived from that one record, so a diagnostic carrying ids its rule does not own fails `typecheck`, and so does one omitting ids its rule always names. See ADR-097.
edits.replace:
`contract/rule.ts` owns what each of those rules is, as one record keyed by that enumeration: the severity it refuses at, and whether it names an `ids` payload. Both are fixed where the rule is defined rather than restated by whoever reports it. `severity` is derived through `ruleSeverity` rather than arriving as a caller-supplied default, and ownership of `ids` is enforced at the producer as the argument list `OwnedIds` derives from the rule it was handed, so a diagnostic carrying ids its rule does not own fails `typecheck`, and so does one omitting ids its rule always names.

It was three variants discriminated by that ownership, and it is one interface because the union was paid for on the public surface and bought nothing on the read side: no production reader pattern-matches a variant, `runtime/patch-registry.ts` compares rule ids for identity and `runtime/refusal.ts` renders them generically. `ids` is optional in the type rather than always present, and that is a measured intermediate state rather than the destination: three raw producers still omit the member, and it becomes required in the slice that converts them. Every diagnostic built through the one constructor in `contract/diagnostics.ts` already carries it, frozen and empty for a rule that names none. See ADR-097.

edits.find: Reading one is unchanged: `path`, `message` and `severity` are on every variant, and `ids` is readable on all three. Two things changed for a caller who writes one down. `ruleId` is a closed union rather than a `string`, so comparing it against a rule this project does not have stops compiling instead of quietly never matching, and constructing a `Diagnostic` of your own with a rule id you invented is refused. And `ids` is present only on the rules that name ids, so a rule that names none cannot carry one. See ADR-097.
edits.replace:
Reading one is simpler than it was: `path`, `message`, `severity` and `ids` are all on it, with no variant to narrow first. Three things are worth knowing if you write one down.

`ruleId` is a closed union rather than a `string`, so comparing it against a rule this project does not have stops compiling instead of quietly never matching, and constructing a `Diagnostic` of your own with a rule id you invented is refused.

`severity` is fixed by the rule rather than by whoever reports it, so a warning rule cannot be reported as an error. It used to default to `"error"` at the constructor, which meant a warning rule reported by a caller that passed nothing became an error diagnostic; the rule answers now.

Whether a rule names `ids` is fixed by the rule too, but it is enforced where a diagnostic is built rather than by the field. A producer takes the payload its rule owns as its argument list, so a rule that names none cannot be handed one and a rule that always names them cannot omit them. The field itself stays optional, and every diagnostic this project builds carries it, frozen and empty for a rule that names none, so `ids` and `ids ?? []` read the same thing.

The three variants that used to express that ownership, `IdlessDiagnostic`, `IdentifiedDiagnostic` and `OptionalIdsDiagnostic`, are removed. A consumer that extended one extends `Diagnostic`. See ADR-097.

edits.find: `ids` is discriminated in three groups rather than per rule, and the groups are ownership rather than arity. A rule that never names ids declares `ids?: undefined`. A rule every construction site names ids at declares `ids` required. A rule whose sites disagree, or that has no construction site to measure, declares it optional. So a diagnostic carrying ids the rule does not own fails `typecheck` rather than being ignored by a reader, and so does one omitting ids its rule always names.
edits.replace:
`ids` ownership is stated per rule, in one record, and it is ownership rather than arity. `contract/rule.ts` answers two questions for every member of the enumeration: the severity the rule refuses at, and whether it names ids. Ownership has two answers and not three. `"sometimes"` was the third and it had exactly two causes, neither of which survived measurement. `observation-source` reported two different refusals under one id and is split: the shape refusal, for a source that is absent, empty or not a string and so has nothing to name, becomes `observation-source-shape` and owns none, while the qualification refusal keeps the id and owns its payload always. And `live-value-key`, `stale-motion-handle` and `stale-track-handle` are minted on thrown error classes with no construction site at all, which is an absent measurement rather than a third answer, so they own none and the first site that forwards one into a diagnostic with a payload fails at the point the decision is owed.

The enforcement is at the producer rather than in the shape of `Diagnostic`, and that is a correction to this record's own first draft. Three variants keyed by ownership were declared, and they were paid for on the public surface, because `Diagnostic` is exported from the package entry. They bought nothing on the read side: no production reader pattern-matches one, `runtime/patch-registry.ts` compares rule ids for identity and `runtime/refusal.ts` renders them generically. So `Diagnostic` is one interface, and what refuses a payload a rule does not own is `OwnedIds` at the call site, derived from that one record. A diagnostic carrying ids the rule does not own still fails `typecheck` rather than being ignored by a reader, and so does one omitting ids its rule always names; the mechanism is the argument list and not the variant, which is the part the first draft put in the wrong place.

`severity` is derived from the same record, through `ruleSeverity`, rather than arriving as a constructor parameter with a default. The default was the literal `"error"`, so a rule's own answer was a suggestion: a caller could overrule it by passing something else and overrode it silently by passing nothing, which made every warning rule reported by such a caller an error diagnostic that nothing noticed. Passing nothing is what almost every caller does.

edits.find: A diagnostic built from a literal rule id, or from one already narrowed to a group as `publishFailureRule` narrows its answer, is checked against its variant by the compiler. The five producers that accept an open `RuleId` still pass through one assertion in `contract/diagnostics.ts`, because TypeScript does not narrow a union by a discriminant it knows only the type of; what changed is that no producer call site reaches that assertion unchecked any more.
edits.replace: A diagnostic is checked at the call site that builds it, against the argument list its rule owns. There is no variant left to be checked against and no narrowing for an assertion to reach: with `Diagnostic` flat, `asDiagnostic` is a widening rather than a correlation stated once, so the "boundary stated rather than implied" this paragraph was written to describe stops describing a union. The widening survives only for the raw producers that still build a frozen object literal of their own, and it is deleted with the last of them.

The derivation is guarded by a one-element tuple on each side of `extends`, because a naked conditional distributes over `RuleId` and would answer with the union of all three lists, which is every existing caller broken rather than one boundary left open.

edits.replace:
A sixth slice followed those five on the same branch, and it is the one that replaced the three variants with one record. `contract/rule.ts` states each rule's severity and its `ids` ownership, `Diagnostic` became one interface, `IdsOwnership` lost its third answer, `observation-source` split into a shape refusal and a qualification refusal, the producers holding a hardcoded `severity: "error"` and a conditional `ids` spread were collapsed into the one constructor, and `contract/diagnostic-ids.ts` was deleted. What it bought over the fourth slice is that a rule answers once: two records answered four rules differently while both existed, so the deletion is what makes the answer single rather than merely primary. It landed in steps, each with its own exact tested SHA on the owning pull request, and the order was forced rather than chosen: while both maps existed a producer had to read `OwnedIds` from whichever module the constructor it forwards to reads, and mixing them was a compile error, so every consumer moved in one request.

The fourth slice also promised that every consumer pattern-matching a rule id would become a total switch, and that half is withdrawn rather than implemented, because it has no subjects.
